Author: @MichaelJLuna
Content:
If Greenland were to pursue independence from Denmark and align with the United States - either as a U.S. territory or through a Compact of Free Association (COFA) - there could be distinct benefits and trade-offs compared to its current relationship with Denmark.

Benefits as a U.S. territory:

Economic Support:  Greenland could receive substantial federal funding from the United States, similar to other territories like Puerto Rico or Guam.  This could include investments in infrastructure, healthcare, and education.

Strategic Development: The United States might prioritize Greenland's development due to its strategic location in the Arctic, which is critical for monitoring geopolitical activities involving Russia and China.

Access to U.S. Markets:  Greenland could benefit from easier access to U.S. markets and trade opportunities, potentially boosting its economy.  

Defense and Security:  As a U.S. territory, Greenland will fall under the protection of the U.S. military, ensuring its security in a geopolitical sensitive region.

Benefits under a COFA:

Sovereignty:  Greenland would retain its independence while benefiting from U.S. financial assistance and defense provisions, similar to the arrangements of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, and Palau.

Military Presence:  The U.S. could establish or expand military bases in Greenland, providing economic benefits through job creation and local spending.

Geopolitical Stability:  A COFA could help Greenland maintain stability and resist external influences from nations like China and Russia.

Comparison to Denmark: 

Current Benefits with Denmark:  Greenland as an autonomous territory of Denmark, already receives significant financial support and has access to the European Union's markets and resources.  Denmark also provides defense and foreign policy support.

Potential Trade-offs:  Aligning with the United States might mean losing some cultural and historical ties with Denmark and the European Union.  Additionally, Greenland would need to carefully negotiate terms to ensure its interests are protected.

Content:
At first watch, this seemed like an informative video with kind of an odd take. Upon further consideration, I had to come back and comment. Lots of strange assumptions...

The conclusion is essentially that only the US can save Greenland from the dystopia it's destined to become. 

If this was just another a short video, I might have considered it somewhat propagandic. I couldn't figure out how they managed to stretch it to 40 minutes. It's almost more like a twisted fantasy.

Content: The only problem I can see regarding potential COFA membership for Greenland. The COFA is an extension of this trusteeship, so the context of having membership is very specific. There is no precedent for the United States to extend membership elsewhere, so it's really down to political will as to whether they'd actually be willing to do this. Nonetheless, if they do agree to it, I think it would be the best option an independent Greenland would have at its disposal. A dual-compact with Denmark may be quite a stretch though, I'd be very surprised if this were ever negotiated.

Author: @minidish
Content:
Canada: The 51st State or a Sovereign Nation? The Choice is Ours

Few Canadians truly appreciate the immense wealth and resources our country possesses. Many don’t realize that, if the total value of what Canada produces were distributed equally, we would be the richest country in the world.

We have energy.
We have water.
We have minerals.
We have fuel.
We have everything a nation needs to thrive—except the collective will of the people to take control of our own prosperity.

So why does it often feel like we are struggling? Why do we remain entangled in systems that limit our sovereignty and keep us dependent?

As discussions of Canada’s future continue—whether it be maintaining sovereignty or integrating more closely with the United States—we must ask ourselves: Do we want to remain in control of our destiny, or will we allow external forces to dictate our future?

The choice is ours.


---

---

Canada’s Potential: Time to Think Bigger

For too long, Canadians have been conditioned to believe that we lack the ability to thrive independently, that we must rely on the United States for our prosperity. But this is a lie—one we’ve told ourselves for far too long.

The reality is that the United States has lost much of its ability to produce, while Canada remains rich in resources, talent, and opportunity. Instead of looking south for guidance, we should be asking ourselves: What do we truly lack?

Yes, we don’t have tropical fruits—we can’t grow mangoes and pineapples in the winter. But that’s no reason to feel limited. There are countless nations south of the U.S. that produce an abundance of fruits and vegetables, and many would welcome a strong, direct trading relationship with Canada. Why not forge those alliances? Why not build stronger economic partnerships that bypass the need to rely on a declining empire?

And when it comes to holidays and warm-weather escapes, why are we still looking to the United States? We have longstanding ties with Cuba and could strengthen relationships with Caribbean nations. If given the opportunity—on fair and respectful terms—some might even consider closer economic or political integration with Canada in exchange for our manufacturing, energy, and industrial support. Of course, such a partnership must be built on mutual respect, ensuring that local cultures and populations remain protected from being overwhelmed.

The truth is, Canada has everything it needs to be great.

We can build world-class cars, planes, rockets, helicopters, and ships. We have the knowledge, the industry, and the raw materials. We can produce great films and television. We have an educated workforce, abundant natural resources, and vast untapped potential. So why do we continue to act like a junior partner to a country that increasingly struggles to sustain itself?

We don’t need a neighbor claiming to “protect” us when, in reality, the biggest threat we face might be that very neighbor. At any moment, if circumstances changed, the United States could march into Canada, overwhelming our nation and taking control.

We also have a vast maritime frontier on the North Atlantic, a strategic advantage we should be more conscious of. Perhaps that’s why the United States has such an interest in Greenland—not for the land itself, but for control over the shipping routes and access to the Arctic. Canada must recognize its own geographic and economic strengths before others decide to claim them for their own.

It’s time for Canadians to wake up. We are not weak. We are not dependent. We are a nation with the power to forge our own path. The only thing holding us back is our own hesitation to embrace our potential.

The future is ours—if we choose to seize it.


---

Content: The population of Greenland, and even of Denmark, does not have the capacity to exercise jurisdiction over the entire island in the emerging future. From this perspective, instead of any independence movement in Greenland seeming to be absurd, it looks more likely to be a program of Russian or even BRICS influence.  Given the small population, and its familiarity with foreign subsidies, it would seem quite easy to buy politicians and votes. Trump's interest in the island, if for no other reason, is to signal to all competitors that the United States is on the island and at its table.  While the islanders deserve to have their homes and commerce and reasonable prospects for autonomous development respected, the islanders claim to all its land is a bit of geographic hubris.

Content:
If I was Canada, I would already have offered Greenland accession as a Province.

Canada (civ-nat) hasn't granted the Inuit territory of Nunavut provincehood (a.k.a. statehood) because of Inuit nationalism and the high likelihood that they'd declare independence once their sovereignty is recognised via elevation to Province (State) status. That's why the Inuit, among others, had to settle for those Final Agreements that are in force under Canada's jurisdiction, which are extensive and probably the best outcome that they could've achieved.
Given the potential for provincehood, the rights and the form of co-sovereignty that the Inuit in Canada seem to have achieved, and the common culture and resource potential, it seems like Canada is the best choice for integrating an independent Greenland from the Inuit perspective. Especially given that the civ-nat USA is not ready to accept (ethnic) nationalism at what would be the state level.

Although Canada holds a similar opinion as the US regarding tribal/ethnic sovereignty at the State level, acquiring Greenland is a unique opportunity for all involved.
The Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (Canada's Inuit advocacy organisation) should be fully supportive of such an effort, because a sovereign Inuit polity being granted confederation as a sovereign ethnic Province would be a game-changer for the 4 Inuit Regions of Canada, which seem to have spent decades moving towards Inuit unification and provincehood.
If Greenland cannot maintain independence, do they have any interest in pan-Inuit nationalism? They are in the best possible negotiating position to achieve and enforce it.

Content:
You completely whiffed on a primary defense reason Trump wants Greenland (or at least unfettered use of large areas of it): Missile Defense.  

Not "early warning" (DUCK!  Russian nukes incoming!); actual defense using missile interceptors that have been in development and even deployment for decades now.  These have been pooh-poohed by "scientists" with no access to the actual engineering for the same decades, but they're getting cheaper and better by the year.  I know, having engineered several of these programs prior to my retirement around a decade ago.  

One of these programs (Ground-Based Midcourse Defense) has an interceptor field in Ft Greeley Alaska, which can only protect the US West coast.  Placing a much larger interceptor field in Greenland would cover the rest of the continental US, and most importantly allow exoatmospheric interceptors with shorter ranges (lower-cost) to be used to intercept ICBMs.  SM-3 interceptors, presently installed on US and Japanese navy ships, are much lower cost than the 40 GMD interceptors at Ft Greeley, which were originally installed to defend against a possible N Korean missile attack.  Installing thousands of SM-3 interceptors in northern Greenland would possibly for the first time ever pose a realistic defense against the Russian nuclear arsenal.

We aren't the slightest bit scared of either the Russian navy, its air forces, nor any of its conventional forces- their failures in the Ukraine invasion have shown all these to be paper Russian bears.  
The ONLY threat to the US from Russia is its nuclear forces, and Greenland would allow missile interceptors to stop Russian ICBMs very early in flight prior to them employing most countermeasures.

Trump also keeps saying he wants to "build an Iron Dome" around the US.  He's not referring literally to the Israeli Iron Dome, a short-range rocket and missile defense, but longer-range missile interceptors like SM-3 or the Israeli Arrow III capable of intercepting ICBMs.  It's a useful analogy, however.  It will require considerable investment in thousands of interceptors, but as I said, they're getting cheaper every year.

Author: @woodchuck003
Content:
Claiming there is no evidence of Chinese influence over the Panama canal is to suggest you like the ability to Google search will excluding current day results. 

Chinese companies have been heavily involved in infrastructure-related contracts in and around the Canal in Panama’s logistics, electricity, and construction sectors. These projects fit naturally with China’s BRI vision, onto which Panama was the first Latin American country to sign in 2018. This, along with Panama’s recognition of China, boosted China’s already existent footprint in the Canal, and Chinese companies have since positioned themselves at either end of the Panama Canal through port concession agreements. In 2016, in a $900 million deal, the China-based Landbridge Group acquired control of Margarita Island, Panama’s largest port on the Atlantic side and in the Colón Free Trade Zone, the largest free trade zone in the Western Hemisphere. The deal established the Panama-Colón Container Port (PCCP) as a deep-water port for megaships, and the construction and expansion was carried out by the China Communications Construction Company (CCCC), a company also active in China’s island-building initiatives in the South China Sea, and the China Harbor Engineering Company (CHEC). The location of the port on the Canal has since allowed China to capitalize on Canal expansion. Additionally, in March 2021 the Panamanian government began the process of renewing the lease of Hutchison Ports PPC, a subsidiary of Hong Kong–based CK Hutchison Holdings, which serves as operator for the ports of Balboa and Cristobal, two major hubs of the Canal’s Pacific and Atlantic outlets, respectively.

Furthermore, in 2018, a Chinese consortium led by CHEC and CCCC announced it was awarded a $1.4 billion contract for the Canal’s fourth bridge, which then-president Varela called “the fifth most important project in the history of the country.” More recently, China Construction Americas finished the Amador Convention Center along the Pacific side of the Canal, a project contracted under the Varela government and funded by Chinese loans. China has also invested in energy-related facilities along the Canal. For example, the Chinese group Shanghai Gorgeous invested $900 million to build a natural gas–fired electricity generation facility. As an economic foothold into Latin America, the Panama Canal is no doubt an important gateway for China’s bid for broader presence and a logistical hub for Chinese goods entering the region.

Aside from infrastructure projects, water management efforts are also a key source of entry for Chinese players. A plan announced in September 2020 would establish a water management system to combat against drought, which threatens the operation of the Canal, but also would impact local access to water for the next 50 years. This presents another opportunity for Chinese investors to increase their presence in Panama beyond the Canal.

Author: @dutchrjen
Content:
A CFOA agreement with the US and Denmark would probably be the best choice.

I've been to Greenland. People do not understand at all how remote and low population the island (or really group of islands) is. 

Most of the Greenlanders live on isolated islands off the main Greenland island with no roads from town to town, most towns do not have airports nor do they have room for airports on the rocky and mountainous terrain, almost none of the towns outside of Nuuk have large enough ports for decent sized ships. This leaves travel between town to town to VERY expensive helicopters or tiny boats. When I was on a cruise ship there we got stuck in some of the fjords because of THOUSANDS of icebergs. We had a super yatch and have a dozen small craft floating behind the cruise ship for protection from the icebergs. The cruise ship had a couple smaller craft helping to guide the cruise ship and the cruise ship was moving at about 2 knots. Even with all of this the cruise ship was constantly bumping into icebergs and we could constantly hear it. Icebergs will be a problem for at least another 100 years regardless of how bad global warming is.

Except for a few small tundra trees in the far south of Greenland the island has no trees. They have to import wood and most of their building materials plus almost everything else except for fish. This is VERY EXPENSIVE.

They need lots of help from larger economies as they are far far far from self-sufficient. 

57,000 people are spread out over a bunch of mostly tiny towns over hundreds of miles of coastline. A lot of this 57,000 will be children, old, not able to work, or in other essential jobs. They simply don't have the population to mine or access the wealth of their island.

They need to get into a better economic block than they have now with better protections. 

CFOA agreements would probably be the best. 

The US isn't going to give Greenland an agreement like this without clear guarantees that Russia and China will not have access. The US will likely allow an agreement where the EU and UK do have access. The current arrangement is very much outdated and makes no sense. It incentivizes Greenland not to develop at all and be dependent on Denmark's subsidies.

Trump has a point, but he is horrible at making that point diplomatically and without pissing everyone off.
